content.text:
When your child runs around even in the library

When your child runs and makes loud noises in quiet places like the library, a restaurant, or the subway, you break into a nervous sweat. Repeating "be quiet" only works for a moment, which is so awkward.

A child not keeping manners isn't a lack of upbringing — it's because they haven't yet felt in their body "why they need to be quiet." Once they understand the reason, children start to be careful on their own.

Curious about the plot of this public manners storybook? Explore the lessons of the public manners storybook along with the illustrations. Meet the key scenes of the public manners story too. content.alt: 44. Here We're Quiet and Gentle - Why public manners matter
content.text:
Why public manners matter

Public manners start from the sense that "there are other people besides me." A child who knows how their actions affect others grows into someone who can be considerate anywhere.

Library manners also lead to an attitude of treasuring books and learning. The experience of quietly focusing builds a child's self-control and helps them naturally learn the rules of living together.
content.caption: A child who knows how their actions affect others learns consideration.

content.alt: 44. Here We're Quiet and Gentle - The story of Hori becoming a Quiet-Quiet Fairy
content.text:
The story of Hori becoming a Quiet-Quiet Fairy

In "Here We're Quiet and Gentle," Hori gets excited and runs around the library, startling friends. But this time, another child's noise makes Hori lose the line he was reading. "Oh, so this is what being disturbed feels like!"

Hori starts the "Quiet-Quiet Fairy game" with Mom. Tiptoe on the toes, whisper softly, hold the book gently with two hands. On the subway ride home, Hori sits nicely too. Together with Hori, your child realizes that "when I'm quiet, others feel comfortable too."
content.caption: The Quiet-Quiet Fairy game turned manners into a fun game.

content.alt: 44. Here We're Quiet and Gentle - The quiet-quiet game to play before going out
content.text:
The quiet-quiet game to play before going out

Before heading to the library or subway, read this book together to let your child know in advance what kind of place it is. When they can anticipate the situation, keeping manners becomes much easier.

Try the "Quiet-Quiet Fairy game" at home. Turning tiptoe walking and soft whispering into a game lets your child practice happily. When they do well, praise them with "You were a truly wonderful Quiet-Quiet Fairy today!" and manners become something to be proud of.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. How do I teach public manners?

A. Let them know, as if it were play, that there are places where we have to be quiet and gentle. Telling them in advance what kind of place it is helps your child prepare their heart.

Q. Does a public manners storybook help?

A. By seeing the main character learn when to stay quiet, your child learns behavior that fits the situation. A public manners storybook naturally nurtures a considerate heart.

Q. What if my child is noisy at a restaurant or library?

A. Rather than scolding, gently explain why we need to be quiet and praise them when they do well. Recognizing that they were nice and quiet leads to the next good behavior.
